B09_00: Regulatory T cell identity is set by a circuit in which RUNX1 with CBFB drives FOXP3 transcription, and FOXP3 then binds RUNX1:CBFB to redirect it. The complex represses effector genes such as IL2 and IFNG while inducing IL-2 receptor alpha, CTLA4 and GITR with NFATC2, and activates CR1, which favours Treg generation. Loss of FOXP3 causes fatal multi-organ autoimmunity, and weakened Treg output contributes to autoimmunity and allergy.
B09_01: RUNX3, with its partner CBFB, binds Runx elements in the distal P1 promoter of RUNX1 and represses it, forming negative cross-regulation between two master regulators of haematopoietic stem cell emergence, lymphocyte and megakaryocyte differentiation and gut epithelial homeostasis. Because both need CBFB, its availability and P1 occupancy determine RUNX1 isoform use. RUNX1 disruption causes familial platelet disorder and leukaemia; RUNX3 silencing is common in gastric cancers.
B09_02: Hippo effectors YAP1 and TAZ partner with TEAD factors to activate growth genes including CCN2, a matricellular protein promoting proliferation, matrix production and fibrosis. RUNX3 binds the TEAD:YAP1 complex and prevents it loading onto the CCN2 promoter, damping transcription. This links RUNX3 tumour suppression to organ-size and contact-inhibition control, explaining why RUNX3 loss in gastric and other epithelial cancers releases YAP-driven expression.
B09_03: Insulin and PI3K/AKT signalling switch off FOXO programmes of stress resistance, autophagy, gluconeogenesis, apoptosis and arrest by exporting the factors from the nucleus. AKT1-3 phosphorylate FOXO1, FOXO3 and FOXO4, exposing a nuclear export signal, and 14-3-3 proteins such as YWHAB, YWHAZ and stratifin retain them in the cytosol, suppressing hepatic glucose production; nuclear FOXO6 is instead inhibited directly. Losing this control contributes to insulin resistance and escape from tumour suppression.
B09_04: RUNX3 with CBFB induces p14-ARF from CDKN2A, which sequesters MDM2 and stabilises p53, creating a barrier against oncogenic transformation by lesions such as mutant KRAS. Induction requires p300 acetylation of RUNX3 and recognition by the bromodomain protein BRD2, while cyclin D1 brings HDAC4 to deacetylate RUNX3 and mute the response, coupling it to the cell cycle. TGF-beta feeds into this node, and RUNX3 silencing is common in gastric cancers.
B09_05: MECP2 reads DNA methylation to tune neuronal gene expression, and its level and activity are controlled at several layers, important because misdosage causes Rett syndrome. miR-132 silences MECP2 mRNA via Argonaute complexes downstream of activity-dependent neurotrophin signalling, and CaMK IV, PKA, HIPK2 and AURKB phosphorylate it to alter chromatin binding and partners. MECP2 represses through NCoR/SMRT and SIN3A-HDAC1/2 or activates with CREB1, and FOXG1 and huntingtin shape its function.
B09_06: NPAS4, an activity-induced neuronal transcription factor that balances excitatory and inhibitory synapses, must appear and disappear rapidly, so its translation is tightly regulated. MicroRNAs including miR-224 and miR-203 repress it through its conserved 3'UTR via the RNA-induced silencing complex: Argonaute bearing the guide, TNRC6 scaffolds recruiting deadenylation and decay machinery, and the helicase MOV10. Losing this restraint disrupts synaptic scaling, memory formation and seizure thresholds.
B09_07: RUNX3 restrains NOTCH signalling, and losing this restraint helps liver cells become tumorigenic. It represses transcription of the NOTCH ligand JAG1, and joins the NICD1-RBPJ-Mastermind coactivator complex with CREBBP/EP300 and KAT2A/B to block activation of HES1, a repressor maintaining progenitor states. This pushes cells toward differentiation rather than proliferation; RUNX3 silencing in hepatocellular carcinoma and gastric cancer releases NOTCH output, linking tumour suppression to cell-fate signalling.
B09_08: RUNX1 with CBFB drives the megakaryocyte gene programme that produces platelets, being induced on megakaryocytic commitment, silenced in erythroid cells and cooperating with GATA1-ZFPM1. PRMT1 arginine methylation favours activation with EP300, KAT2B and WDR5 complexes, whereas unmethylated RUNX1 represses with SIN3A/B, HDAC1 and PRMT6. Targets include ITGA2B, GP1BA, THBS1, PF4, MYL9, PRKCQ, NFE2, NR4A3 and MIR27A, which feeds back on RUNX1; loss causes familial platelet disorder and leukaemia predisposition.
B09_09: Beyond osteoblast differentiation, RUNX2 with CBFB drives a migratory and invasive programme in bone and in tumour cells colonising it. It activates ITGA5 for fibronectin attachment, ITGBL1, which modulates TGF-beta and aids bone metastasis, and the collagenase MMP13, which lets immune and cancer cells traverse matrix. AKT phosphorylation boosts RUNX2 activity, linking PI3K signalling to migration, and the same targets aid retinal angiogenesis and stem cell migration.
B09_10: MECP2, a methyl-CpG-binding nuclear protein, regulates other regulators, acting on promoters of CREB1, MEF2C, RBFOX1 and PPARG to set the tone of activity-dependent neuronal maturation, synapse refinement and dendritic complexity. Because it can repress or activate, its loss shifts a whole regulatory layer, explaining Rett syndrome, with regression after apparently normal early development, and equally damaging duplications. The PPARG connection extends its influence to adipocyte differentiation and metabolic programmes.
B09_11: RUNX2, known for osteoblast commitment, also acts in the myeloid programme by stimulating transcription of LGALS3 together with RUNX1 and the shared partner CBFB, which stabilises DNA binding. Galectin-3 rises as myeloid progenitors mature and contributes to adhesion, phagocyte behaviour and inflammation. This links lineage-specifying transcription to disease, as galectin-3 is abundant in pituitary tumours and glioma and RUNX1-CBFB disruption recurs in leukaemia.
B09_12: RUNX1, master regulator of definitive haematopoiesis, is controlled at many layers that determine stem cell emergence and lineage maturation; haploinsufficiency causes familial platelet disorder and translocations drive acute myeloid leukaemia. It is transcribed from two alternative promoters, and microRNAs such as miR-17, miR-20a, miR-18a and miR-27a limit translation via Argonaute-TNRC6. CBFB heterodimerisation enables DNA binding, opposed by D-type cyclins and CDK6, PTPN11 reverses SRC-family phosphorylation, and PML directs subnuclear localisation.
B09_13: The AP-2 factors TFAP2A, TFAP2B and TFAP2C regulate growth factor and receptor genes that govern epithelial and placental proliferation. They activate ESR1, ERBB2, EGFR, KIT and TGFA but repress VEGFA, with YY1 enhancing ERBB2 transcription and ATAD2 aiding activation, and in placenta they drive both chorionic gonadotropin subunits. TFAP2C overexpression in estrogen-receptor-positive breast and endometrial tumours makes this circuitry a determinant of hormone-responsive tumour phenotype.
B09_14: MECP2 directly activates transcription of GAD1 and GAD2, whose enzymes convert glutamate to GABA, placing this methylation reader upstream of excitation-inhibition balance. Loss of MECP2 from GABAergic neurons lowers GABA and reproduces Rett-like breathing irregularity, stereotypies and motor and social deficits, while loss in parvalbumin interneurons blunts sensory responses, impairs motor learning and disrupts interneuron maturation and expression of parvalbumin, GABA-A subunits and potassium channels, linking epigenetics to neurodevelopmental disease.
B09_15: When insulin is low, FOXO1, FOXO3, FOXO4 and FOXO6 escape AKT restraint and directly control metabolism, oxidative defence and neuronal programmes. They induce gluconeogenic PCK1 and G6PC1, repress glucokinase via SIN3A-HDAC and SREBF1, and tune IGFBP1 and resistin; in hypothalamus they raise NPY and AGRP and repress POMC. With PPARGC1A, SIRT3 and ataxin-3 they induce SOD2 and catalase, and drive FBXO32 and TRIM63 in muscle wasting.
B09_16: NPAS4 is an activity-induced transcription factor linking neuronal excitation to excitatory-inhibitory synapse balance, plasticity, contextual memory, neuroprotection after seizure or ischaemia, and beta-cell insulin expression. It dimerises with ARNT, ARNT2 or BMAL1 and recruits CREBBP, with MAPK1/3 and nuclear export shaping its activity and short half-life. Targets include CDK5, CDK5R1, RBFOX3 and RET for maturation, BDNF, IQSEC3, PLK2, SYT10 and FOS for synaptic function, and NAMPT.
B09_17: TGF-beta can trigger apoptosis by inducing BIM: RUNX3 activates BCL2L11 transcription together with SMAD3, SMAD4 and FOXO3. BIM neutralises anti-apoptotic BCL2 proteins and promotes BAX/BAK-dependent mitochondrial permeabilisation, committing cells to intrinsic apoptosis. This contributes to TGF-beta tumour suppression in epithelial and gastric tissue and to lymphocyte culling, and RUNX3 methylation or SMAD loss lets cells survive that should be eliminated.
B09_18: RUNX3, an epithelial tumour suppressor directing lymphocyte and dendritic cell differentiation, is regulated at several levels; CpG methylation or hypoxia silences it in gastric tumours. Transcription responds to TGF-beta/SMAD and autoregulation, with alternative promoters and splicing giving distinct isoforms. RUNX3 needs CBFB to bind DNA and EP300 to activate targets such as CDKN2A, while SRC phosphorylation blocks nuclear entry and MDM2 and SMURF ligases drive its degradation.
B09_19: When insulin and growth factor signals fall, nuclear FOXO1, FOXO3 and FOXO4 enforce quiescence by inducing p21, p27, RBL2/p130, CCNG2, BTG1, GADD45A, caveolin-1 and KLF4. This withdrawal into G0 restrains erythroid progenitors, lymphocytes and telencephalic neuroepithelial progenitors, where FOXG1 opposes it. SMAD2/3-SMAD4 from TGF-beta signalling partners with FOXO to induce p21 and, in muscle, myostatin, and loss of this arm removes a tumour-suppressive brake and promotes stem cell exhaustion.
B09_20: RUNX1 with CBFB, a blood lineage regulator often altered in leukaemia, directly transcribes WNT pathway components and so sets WNT signalling strength, which governs self-renewal versus differentiation. With FOXP3 as cofactor it induces RSPO3, a WNT-potentiating R-spondin with oncogenic activity in breast; with ligand-activated estrogen receptor alpha it induces AXIN1, a destruction-complex scaffold restraining beta-catenin. Hormonal and immune context thus determines whether RUNX1 amplifies or dampens WNT.
B09_21: RUNX2 is the master regulator of osteoblast differentiation, and its dosage matters: haploinsufficiency causes cleidocranial dysplasia, while sustained activity drives mineralisation and chondrocyte maturation. Transcription from two promoters is stimulated by estrogen receptor alpha, DLX5, DLX6 and TWIST1, repressed by NR3C1, MSX2 and NKX3-2, and switched by ERR-alpha depending on PGC1 partner. Protein control includes CBFB binding, STAT1 sequestration and ubiquitination by SMURF1, WWP1, STUB1 and SKP2 ligases before degradation.
B09_22: RUNX2 with CBFB commits mesenchymal progenitors to osteoblasts and drives genes for mineralised matrix, including type I collagen, osteocalcin and UCMA; its loss causes cleidocranial dysplasia. It cooperates with SP7 and SATB2 and is regulated extensively: MAPK phosphorylation promotes and SRC/YES1-dependent YAP1 binding restrains osteocalcin activation, androgen receptor and HDACs block DNA binding, HEY1, HES1 and ZNF521 repress it, and ubiquitination limits abundance, linking skeletal development, hormones and matrix production.
B09_23: TGF-beta growth arrest requires p21, and RUNX3 induces CDKN1A by binding and cooperating with TGFB1-activated SMAD3:SMAD4 at its promoter, reinforced by ZFHX3. This is especially important in gastric epithelium: Runx3-deficient mice are TGF-beta-insensitive and develop gastric hyperplasia, and RUNX3 silencing recurs in gastric cancer. RUNX3 also coactivates TP53, boosting p53 targets including CDKN1A and linking cytokine- and damage-driven cell cycle arrest.
B09_24: Part of the B cell receptor signalling apparatus is set up transcriptionally before antigen exposure, as RUNX1 with CBFB activates genes such as BLK, a kinase propagating receptor engagement into cascades driving B cell development, differentiation and antibody responses. At the BLK promoter RUNX1 cooperates with ETS factors ELF1 and ELF2 and with the B lineage factor PAX5. This shows how haematopoietic transcription factors specify signalling competence.
B09_25: Retinoic acid drives cells out of cycle into differentiation partly by repressing growth genes. TFAP2A accumulates after treatment and acts as a repressor with nucleophosmin (NPM1), likely recruiting HDAC1 and HDAC2 to deacetylate promoters of HSPD1, NOP2 and MYBL2, the latter two being proliferation markers. The complex also represses the NPM1 promoter, consistent with falling NPM1 levels, creating a self-limiting loop linking retinoid signalling to proliferative withdrawal.
B09_26: RUNX1 with CBFB shapes haematopoietic cytokine responsiveness by inducing the leukemia inhibitory factor receptor, which transmits IL-6 family signals involved in blood production, implantation, placental development and neural differentiation. With the ETS coactivator ELF1 it also drives interleukin-3, a growth factor for multipotent and myeloid progenitors. Disruption of RUNX1 or CBFB in familial platelet disorder and acute leukaemia translocations leaves progenitors with miscalibrated responses to interleukin cues.
B09_27: AP-2 factors govern neural crest, craniofacial, limb, skin and placental development; TFAP2A and TFAP2B mutations cause branchio-oculo-facial and Char syndromes, and TFAP2C drives trophoblast and germ cell identity and is co-amplified with HER2. Activation requires dimerisation via the helix-span-helix motif and binding to GC-rich palindromes. CITED co-factors, especially CITED2, recruit EP300 and CREBBP, YEATS4 enhances TFAP2B binding, WWOX sequesters AP-2, and CITED2 loss reproduces neural crest, cardiac and adrenal defects.
B09_28: RUNX3 restrains WNT-driven proliferation, explaining its tumour suppressor role in gastrointestinal epithelium. Stabilised beta-catenin partners with TCF7, TCF7L1, TCF7L2 and LEF1 to induce cyclin D1 and MYC, which drive G1 progression. RUNX3 binds the beta-catenin:TCF/LEF complex and prevents its occupancy of CCND1 and MYC promoters without affecting beta-catenin stabilisation, so RUNX3 silencing or mislocalisation promotes proliferation and gastric and colon carcinogenesis.
B09_29: Acetylation helps determine whether stressed cells mount antioxidant and repair responses, arrest, or die via FOXO factors. Under oxidative stress CBP, p300 and PCAF acetylate FOXO1, FOXO3 and FOXO4, changing promoter preference and nuclear retention and potentially overriding insulin-driven exclusion; SIRT1 and SIRT3 deacetylate them, linking output to energy and redox state, with thioredoxin and TXNIP adding thiol control. This axis governs stress resistance, metabolism, muscle atrophy and tumour suppression.
B09_30: RUNX1 with CBFB binds ligand-activated estrogen receptor alpha in breast epithelium and co-occupies regulatory regions of a subset of estrogen targets, including GPAM, KCTD6 and AXIN1. This gives RUNX1 influence over which genes respond to estrogen, connecting hormone signalling to lipid metabolism and Wnt regulation beyond proliferation. RUNX1 is a recurrently altered tumour suppressor in estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer, and high GPAM expression correlates with better survival.
B09_31: RUNX1 with CBFB instructs myeloid progenitors toward granulocyte, monocyte, erythroid and megakaryocyte fates, recruiting CREBBP to open chromatin at target promoters. Targets include CSF2 (GM-CSF), supporting myeloid growth, survival and maturation; LGALS3, whose galectin-3 rises with maturation; and PRKCB, regulating myeloid apoptosis. Because this programme balances self-renewal and differentiation, RUNX1 or CBFB loss or translocation stalls maturation and causes acute myeloid leukaemia and familial platelet disorders.
B09_32: MECP2 directly regulates neuronal receptors, channels and transporters, and because both loss (Rett syndrome) and duplication are harmful, target dosage matters. Targets include GRIA2, GRIN2A and GRIN2B for excitatory transmission, opioid receptors OPRK1 and OPRM1, MET, NOTCH1, TRPC3 and SLC2A3. MECP2 activates with CREB1 or represses via SIN3A with HDAC1 and HDAC2, while phosphatases PTPN1 and PTPN4 indirectly modulate receptor kinase signalling.
B09_33: RUNX3 with CBFB shapes immune identity and leukocyte adhesion. It induces RORC to drive ILC1 and ILC3 development for mucosal defence, and activates ITGAL (CD11a) and ITGA4 (CD49d), which mediate transendothelial migration and T cell costimulation. A Runt-domain-lacking isoform accumulating in maturing monocyte-derived dendritic cells cannot transactivate these genes and dampens inflammation, and RUNX3 induction of osteopontin (SPP1) links this programme to pancreatic cancer invasiveness.
B09_34: In keratinocytes, RUNX1 with CBFB shifts the balance between stem cell maintenance and differentiation by repressing a few targets. It represses SERPINB13, an inhibitor of cathepsins L and V acting in epidermal differentiation and often lost in head and neck cancer, and SOCS3 and SOCS4, raising STAT3 activity. Elevated STAT3 promotes proliferation and self-renewal in hair follicle and epithelial stem cells, implicating this circuit in skin squamous cell carcinoma.
B09_35: RUNX1 with CBFB, master regulator of definitive haematopoiesis, recruits chromatin co-factors whose net effect on targets can be activating or repressive depending on context. HIPK2 phosphorylates RUNX1 and bound EP300, a step disrupted by leukaemia-associated CBFB mutations. The complex binds PRC1 subunits RING1/RNF2, CBX and PHC proteins, contacts SWI/SNF subunits SMARCA4, SMARCB1 and ARID1A for nucleosome remodelling, and receives casein kinase 2 phosphorylation, linking gene control to chromatin state.
B09_36: During endochondral ossification, RUNX2 with CBFB controls the switch from chondrocyte proliferation to hypertrophy by inducing Indian hedgehog and hypertrophic markers such as type X collagen, coupling maturation to the PTHrP feedback loop that sets growth plate length. GLI2 transduces hedgehog signals and HDAC4 restrains RUNX2; losing HDAC4 causes premature ossification, while RUNX2 loss blocks maturation and limb elongation. RUNX2 also governs osteoblasts, and its haploinsufficiency causes cleidocranial dysplasia.
B09_37: Without growth factor and insulin signalling, FOXO factors enter the nucleus and induce cell death genes, pruning NGF-deprived neurons, eliminating enteric precursors lacking RET signalling and underpinning FOXO tumour suppression, which PI3K/AKT activity in cancer blocks. Targets include BIM, PUMA, FASLG, BCL6, PINK1 and STK11. CREBBP, EP300 and NF-Y cooperate at these promoters while CITED2 and DDIT3 modulate the response, linking nutrient and stress sensing to cell death decisions.
B09_38: RUNX1 with CBFB binds the promoters of ZO-1, occludin and claudin-5 and increases their expression, coordinating production of the scaffold and membrane proteins that form endothelial and epithelial tight junctions. In brain endothelium these form the blood-brain and blood-tumour barrier, and when miR-18a represses RUNX1 in glioma, junctions loosen and permeability rises. This links a haematopoietic transcription factor to endothelial barrier integrity and drug delivery to tumours.
B09_39: TFAP2A and TFAP2C, as homo- and possibly heterodimers, cooperate with the coactivator CITED2 to induce PITX2, a homeodomain factor that establishes left-right asymmetry and directs cardiac outflow tract and valve formation. Loss of this input reproduces laterality defects and congenital heart malformations seen with CITED2 or AP-2 disruption, and TFAP2A mutation causes branchio-oculo-facial syndrome. It illustrates how AP-2 factors convert positional signals into downstream regulatory programmes.
B09_40: AP-2 factors control the p21 CDK inhibitor gene, which restrains G1/S progression and mediates growth arrest and senescence, a balance often skewed in tumours. TFAP2A binds and activates the CDKN1A promoter, whereas TFAP2C represses it by recruiting MYC and the demethylase KDM5B to remove activating histone methylation. The relative abundance of these paralogues thus sets p21 levels, linking developmental transcription programmes to cell cycle entry and differentiation-associated exit.
B09_41: NPAS4, induced within minutes of neuronal activity to tune inhibitory synapse number, is regulated transcriptionally. Calcium entry activates it via SRF and PI3K/AKT, while calcium-free DREAM (KCNIP3) silences it at rest and REST represses it in non-neuronal cells and limits its duration in neurons. Glucocorticoid-bound NR3C1, histone deacetylases and CpG methylation further gate the locus, and dysregulation disturbs excitatory-inhibitory balance, memory, and stress-related and neurodegenerative processes in the hippocampus.
B09_42: AP-2 factors directing neural crest, craniofacial, limb, skin and mammary development are actively restrained. KCTD1 and KCTD15 bind the AP-2 transactivation domain and block activation, and KCTD1 mutation causes scalp-ear-nipple syndrome with renal defects. UBE2I-mediated SUMO1 conjugation weakens TFAP2A, TFAP2B and TFAP2C, affecting epithelial differentiation and breast cancer stem cell traits, and WWOX sequesters TFAP2C outside the nucleus; both excess and deficient AP-2 activity distort development.
B09_43: RUNX1 with CBFB helps blood stem cells commit to lineages, notably by recruiting KMT2A to the SPI1 promoter to deposit H3K4 trimethylation, inducing PU.1, which limits self-renewal and enables myeloid and lymphoid commitment. RUNX1 also joins a TAL1 complex with LMO1/LMO2, LDB1, GATA factors and E-proteins that drives MYB, promoting proliferation and survival in T-ALL. ITCH and proteasomal degradation limit RUNX1, whose loss causes familial platelet disorder and AML.
B09_44: MECP2, whose loss causes Rett syndrome, sets expression of neuronal secreted ligands shaping synapses and circuits: BDNF for synaptic maturation and plasticity, corticotropin-releasing hormone for stress and anxiety, somatostatin marking inhibitory interneurons, and DLL1 affecting progenitor fate. It represses via SIN3A-HDAC1 histone deacetylation or activates with CREB1 in an activity-dependent manner. Because ligand dosage is tuned, both loss and duplication of MECP2 cause neurodevelopmental disease.
